name: Liuli glazed roof tile
summary: Glazed roof tiles in yellow, green and blue that the imperial kilns made for the palaces and temples of Beijing. Rank and meaning decide the colour: imperial yellow covers the main halls of the Forbidden City.

philosophy.core_thesis: A roof tile is a sign of rank: its colour, its ridge figures and its curved line tell the viewer which hall is for the emperor.
design_principles: Glaze the main halls in yellow, the princes' houses in green and the Temple of Heaven in blue.
Cover the roof with half-round tiles and flat tiles in rows, and finish the eave with a round disc tile.
Place a row of glazed animals on each hip ridge; use up to 9 figures for the highest hall.
Mould each ridge piece, finial and dragon in a mould, and glaze it in the colour of the roof.
Curve the eaves up at the corner, so that the tile line follows a soft S shape.
Press the tile from a fine, pure clay and fire it twice: once bare, once with the lead glaze.
Build a glazed screen wall with moulded relief tiles, as in the Nine-Dragon Wall.
anti_patterns: A matt grey or brown roof tile with no glaze
Random mixed colours with no rank
A flat roof or a roof of metal sheet
Ridge figures that copy a Western gargoyle
A thin, even glaze with no pooling at the edges

form.shape: Half-round cover tiles and flat pan tiles, eave discs with a dragon or a flower, ridge pieces, ridge-end beasts and moulded relief tiles for wall panels.
form.profile: A long curved tile with a gentle taper; the pan tile is a shallow arc and the cover tile a half cylinder that sits over the joint.
form.foot_and_rim: The eave tile ends in a round disc or a drop-shaped apron with a moulded face; the ridge ends in a large beast with a back hole for the fixing.
form.proportion: A pan tile is about 40 to 60 cm long and 2 to 3 cm thick; a main ridge end for a great hall stands about 3 m high.
rules: Use one glaze colour on one hall.
Put the same animals along each hip in a set order.
Mould the ornament; do not carve it after the glaze.
Seal the joint of the tiles with a cover tile.

bodies.rule: Use a fine, pale clay that stays pure of iron and grit, so that the lead glaze keeps a clean yellow. The tile must be hard, but it must stay porous.

methods: pressing into plaster and wooden moulds
wire cutting of the half-round tile
forming.joins: Tiles lap over each other and sit in a bed of lime mortar on the roof; ridge pieces are stacked on an iron rod and fixed with mortar.
forming.details: A small hole for the nail on each eave disc, thick glaze on the underside of the curve, and a dark body edge on the cut face.

glaze.pattern: Plain yellow, green or blue roofs, with a row of glazed dragons, phoenixes and lions on the ridge and tile reliefs of dragons on the screen walls.
glaze.gloss: High gloss, about 80 to 95 GU; the lead glaze is thick, bright and a little wavy on the half-round tile.
glaze.wear: The glaze keeps its colour for centuries; at an edge it crazes and shows the pale body; ridge beasts lose a small horn or tail.

palette.strategy: Imperial yellow, jade green and peacock blue as flat colour fields; the colour marks rank, and the white-grey wall and red column below frame it.

firing.kiln: A brick kiln that burns wood or coal; the tile sits in saggars or in stacked rows, with a bisque firing first and a glaze firing second.
processes: pressing and drying of the tile
dipping or brushing with lead glaze with a copper, iron or cobalt colour
a glaze firing at about 900 to 1000 °C
firing.scale: Imperial kilns near Beijing made tiles for the Forbidden City, with more than 9,000 rooms; each roof used thousands of pieces.
firing.signs: A maker stamp on the back of an eave tile, glaze drips at the lower edge, and a small gap in the colour where the tile rested in the kiln.

pieces.form: Half-round cover tile in imperial yellow with a wave of lead glaze
Row of glazed hip-ridge beasts: a rider, a dragon and a lion
Large ridge-end beast with an open mouth that bites the ridge
Screen wall panel with a coiling dragon in green, blue and yellow

positive: Chinese imperial yellow glazed roof tile
curved eaves on a palace hall
dragon relief on a screen wall
lead glaze in yellow green and blue
red wall and white marble base
museum or travel photograph in clear light

evidence.title: Manchu Forbidden City Roof Tile Ends.jpg

emotion.target_response: Ceremony and rank: the viewer sees a bright roof over a red wall and reads the order of the court in its colours.

use_cases: an image of a Chinese palace or temple with the right roof colour
a tile or roof-detail brief with glazed ridge animals
a label on Ming and Qing glazed architectural ceramics
avoid_when: the brief needs a modern flat roof
the brief is for an unglazed, earth-coloured roof
the brief needs a European roof tile

modifiers.how: Change the tile to a moulded brick, use an alkaline glaze in blue, and set the animals in rows on a wall.
Change to a white tin glaze with blue and a figure scene, and frame it with a wreath of fruit.

ornament_level.note: The rank of the hall sets the colour and the number of ridge figures.

wall_thickness.note: Tile thickness is 2 to 3 cm; a ridge beast has a thicker wall of 3 to 4 cm.
